title: States of Matter
description: All matter is made of tiny particles. Solids have particles packed tightly in a fixed shape. Liquids flow and take the shape of their container. Gases spread to fill any space.

exercises.question: In a SOLID, how are the particles arranged?
choices: packed tightly and vibrating in fixed positions
exercises.exp: Solid particles are packed tightly together. They vibrate but do not move around — that is why solids keep their shape.

exercises.question: In a LIQUID, the particles ___.
choices: are far apart with no attraction
flow and slide past each other
exercises.exp: Liquid particles are close together but can slide past each other — that is why liquids flow!

exercises.question: In a GAS, the particles ___.
choices: move rapidly and spread far apart
exercises.exp: Gas particles zoom around rapidly in all directions and spread out to fill any container.

exercises.question: Which state of matter has both a fixed SHAPE and fixed VOLUME?
exercises.exp: Solids have a fixed shape AND fixed volume — a rock is always the same shape and size.

exercises.question: Which state of matter has a fixed VOLUME but NO fixed shape?
exercises.exp: Liquids take the shape of their container but always have the same volume — pour juice into any glass!

exercises.question: Which state of matter has NEITHER a fixed shape nor fixed volume?
exercises.exp: Gases expand to fill whatever container they are in — they have no fixed shape or volume.

exercises.question: Classify: lava flowing from a volcano
exercises.exp: Lava is molten rock — it flows like a very slow, thick liquid.

exercises.question: Which two items are both SOLIDS?
choices: a rock and an ice cube
exercises.exp: Both a rock and an ice cube have a fixed shape and volume — they are solids!

exercises.question: When you COMPRESS (squeeze) a gas into a smaller space, what happens?
choices: the particles get forced closer together
exercises.exp: Gas can be compressed — the particles are pushed closer together. Bike tires and scuba tanks use compressed gas!

exercises.question: Why does perfume SPREAD across a room?
choices: perfume particles are a gas that diffuse through the air
exercises.exp: Perfume evaporates into tiny gas particles that spread through the air — that is how you smell it across the room!

exercises.question: Water, ice, and steam are all ___.
choices: the same substance in different states
exercises.exp: Water, ice, and steam are all H₂O — just in different states (liquid, solid, gas).

exercises.question: Which state of matter is EASIEST to compress?
exercises.exp: Gases are easily compressed because there is lots of empty space between the widely-spread particles.

exercises.question: Why does a SOLID keep its own shape even when placed in a container?
choices: because solid particles are locked in fixed positions and vibrate in place
exercises.exp: Solid particles vibrate but cannot move from their fixed positions — that is why solids hold their shape!

exercises.question: Why does LIQUID take the shape of its container?
choices: liquid particles are fixed like a solid
liquid particles can slide past each other, flowing to fill any shape
exercises.exp: Liquid particles attract each other but can slide past — they flow to fill the bottom of any container they are poured into.

exercises.question: Air is a GAS. What happens when you open a perfume bottle in a room?
choices: the perfume particles stay near the bottle
perfume gas particles spread throughout the room due to diffusion
the perfume becomes a liquid on the floor
exercises.exp: Gas particles move rapidly and spread out (diffuse) to fill the space — that is why you can smell perfume across a room!

exercises.question: Which observation tells you a substance is a LIQUID?
choices: it has a fixed shape and cannot be poured
it flows and takes the shape of its container but has a definite volume
it expands to fill any container completely
it is always transparent and colourless
exercises.exp: Liquids pour and flow (no fixed shape) but do NOT expand to fill all available space (they have fixed volume).

exercises.question: Which observation tells you a substance is a GAS?
choices: it expands to fill the entire container it is in
it sinks to the bottom of a container
exercises.exp: Gases expand to completely fill any container. Pour a gas into a larger container and it spreads to fill all of it!

exercises.question: A balloon is filled with helium gas. What happens to the gas when the balloon is squeezed?
choices: the gas particles get pushed closer together — it is compressed
exercises.exp: Gas is compressible — squeezing the balloon forces gas particles closer together into a smaller space.

exercises.question: Honey flows slowly. Water flows quickly. Both are LIQUIDS. What explains the difference?
choices: honey has stronger attractions between particles — it is more viscous
exercises.exp: Viscosity measures how easily a liquid flows. Honey has high viscosity (flows slowly); water has low viscosity (flows easily).

exercises.question: ICE, WATER, and STEAM are the same substance. How do their particle arrangements differ?
choices: ice = tightly packed fixed; water = sliding past; steam = fast and far apart
all three have the same particle arrangement
steam is tightly packed and ice is spread apart
exercises.exp: Same H₂O molecules, three arrangements: ice (fixed grid), water (sliding), steam (fast, far apart) — state depends on energy!

exercises.question: A scientist cools a gas slowly. First it becomes a ___, then a ___.
exercises.exp: Cooling removes energy: gas → liquid (condensation) → solid (freezing). First it condenses, then freezes.

exercises.question: Why are SOLIDS generally denser than gases?
choices: solids are always heavier per atom
solid particles are packed tightly with little space between them; gas particles are far apart
density has nothing to do with particles
exercises.exp: Density depends on how tightly particles are packed. Solids are tightly packed → high density. Gas particles are far apart → low density.

exercises.question: Oxygen gas (O₂) can be stored in a steel CYLINDER under high pressure. Why can it be compressed into a small cylinder?
choices: oxygen becomes a solid under pressure
gas particles have large empty spaces between them that can be squeezed out under pressure
exercises.exp: Gas particles are mostly empty space. Under high pressure, those spaces shrink — allowing large amounts of gas to be stored in small cylinders!

exercises.question: A swimmer blows air underwater, making bubbles. The bubbles rise because ___.
choices: air (gas) is less dense than water (liquid) and floats upward
water pushes air down then releases it
exercises.exp: Air bubbles are much less dense than water — buoyancy pushes them upward through the denser liquid to the surface.

exercises.question: LIQUID NITROGEN is nitrogen gas cooled to -196°C. At that temperature nitrogen is a liquid. What does this tell us?
choices: with enough cooling (energy removed), even gases can become liquids
temperature has no effect on state
exercises.exp: All substances can exist in all states — given extreme enough temperatures. Nitrogen gas becomes liquid at -196°C!

exercises.question: In which state of matter do particles have the MOST energy?
exercises.exp: Gas particles have the most energy — they move the fastest and are most spread out. Solid particles have the least energy.

exercises.question: A SOLID has a definite shape and a definite volume. What does DEFINITE VOLUME mean?
choices: it can expand to fill any space
it always occupies the same amount of space regardless of the container
its volume changes with temperature only
volume is not a property of solids
exercises.exp: Definite volume means the substance takes up the same amount of space no matter what container it is in — unlike gas, which expands!

exercises.question: Mercury is a METAL that is a LIQUID at room temperature. This is unusual because most metals are ___.
exercises.exp: Almost all metals are solid at room temperature. Mercury is unique — it melts at -39°C, so it is liquid at room temperature!

exercises.question: You blow up a balloon and tie it. If you put it in a FREEZER, it shrinks. Why?
choices: the rubber gets heavier in the cold
cold temperature reduces gas particle speed — they take up less space
the balloon absorbs water from the freezer
air escapes through the balloon wall
exercises.exp: Cooler gas particles move more slowly and push less on the balloon walls — the balloon shrinks as gas volume decreases with temperature.

exercises.question: LIQUID and GAS are both fluids. What does FLUID mean?
choices: a substance that is always clear
a substance that is always wet
a substance that is always cold
exercises.exp: Fluids flow — both liquids and gases are fluids. Solids cannot flow. That is why liquids pour and gases spread!

exercises.question: When you pump up a bicycle tire, you push MORE gas into the SAME space. The tire gets firm. This demonstrates that gas ___.
choices: can be compressed — more gas particles can be squeezed into the same volume
becomes a liquid inside the tire
loses its gas properties under pressure
exercises.exp: Gas compression allows many more particles into the same space — pumped-up tires hold compressed air that creates outward pressure!

exercises.question: PLASMA is a fourth state of matter found in stars and lightning. It is like a gas but ___.
choices: the particles are uncharged and slow
particles carry electrical charge — it conducts electricity
exercises.exp: Plasma is super-heated gas where particles become electrically charged — making it conduct electricity. The sun is mostly plasma!

exercises.question: The three common states of matter differ in how their particles are ___.
choices: arranged and how freely they move
exercises.exp: Particles in solids: tightly packed and vibrate; liquids: close but flow; gases: far apart and move fast. Arrangement determines state!

exercises.question: At ABSOLUTE ZERO (−273°C), particles have the minimum possible energy. What happens to matter?
choices: all particles stop moving completely and matter enters its lowest energy state
exercises.exp: Absolute zero (0 Kelvin, −273°C) is the coldest possible temperature — particles have minimum kinetic energy. Nothing can be colder than this!

exercises.question: The KINETIC PARTICLE THEORY explains that all particles in matter ___.
choices: are in constant motion — even in solids, particles vibrate
only move in liquids and gases
have no energy at room temperature
exercises.exp: Kinetic theory: all particles are always moving. Solids vibrate in place; liquids flow; gases zip around at high speed. Temperature = average kinetic energy!

exercises.question: Why does a solid MELT when heated?
choices: heat adds particles to the solid
added thermal energy causes particles to vibrate faster until they overcome the forces holding them in fixed positions
melting removes mass from the solid
heat always causes a chemical change
exercises.exp: Heat gives particles more energy → they vibrate harder → eventually break free of their fixed positions → solid melts into liquid!

exercises.question: Which property is TRUE for SOLIDS but NOT for liquids or gases?
choices: they maintain a definite shape without needing a container
exercises.exp: Only solids maintain their own fixed shape. Liquids take the container's shape; gases fill any available space completely.

exercises.question: As you heat a gas, its particles ___.
choices: speed up and spread further apart (if allowed to expand)
turn back into a liquid immediately
exercises.exp: Heating increases particle kinetic energy — particles move faster. If the gas can expand, it spreads out. If confined (like a sealed container), pressure increases!

exercises.question: What is VISCOSITY?
choices: a measure of how resistant a liquid is to flowing — how thick or runny it is
the temperature at which a liquid boils
exercises.exp: Viscosity is how thick and slow-flowing a liquid is. Honey has high viscosity (flows slowly); water has low viscosity (flows easily).

exercises.question: Honey flows SLOWLY; water flows QUICKLY. Which has higher VISCOSITY?
choices: honey — it is thicker and resists flowing
viscosity cannot be compared between liquids
exercises.exp: Honey has much higher viscosity than water — its molecules are larger and more tangled, creating more resistance to flow.

exercises.question: A sealed metal can is heated in a fire. The pressure inside increases. Why?
choices: gas particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often, increasing pressure
the can draws in air from outside
exercises.exp: Temperature increases kinetic energy → gas particles slam the walls harder and more frequently → pressure rises. This can cause the can to burst!

exercises.question: Which state of matter is LEAST compressible?
choices: solid — its particles are already tightly packed with almost no space
exercises.exp: Solids are nearly incompressible — particles are already touching. Gases compress easily (lots of empty space). Liquids are slightly compressible.

exercises.question: GEL (like hair gel) behaves like a solid at rest but can be smeared. What type of material is it?
choices: a non-Newtonian material — it does not follow standard liquid or solid rules
exercises.exp: Gels, toothpaste, and custard are non-Newtonian — their viscosity changes under stress. They blur the line between solid and liquid!

exercises.question: Why does an inflated balloon SHRINK in cold weather?
choices: the rubber contracts and squeezes the air out
gas particles slow down, taking up less space — the volume decreases in the cold
the balloon gains mass in cold air
cold air enters through the rubber
exercises.exp: In cold air, gas particles slow down and occupy less space — the balloon deflates slightly. Warm up the balloon and it reinflates!

exercises.question: SURFACE TENSION allows some insects to walk on water. Surface tension is caused by ___.
choices: cohesive forces between water molecules at the surface creating a 'skin'
air pushing the insect up from below
exercises.exp: Water molecules attract each other (cohesion) — molecules at the surface are pulled inward, creating a 'skin'. Small insects can walk on this!

exercises.question: What is SUBLIMATION?
choices: a solid melting to a liquid
a liquid evaporating to a gas
a solid changing directly to a gas without becoming a liquid first
a gas condensing to a solid
exercises.exp: Sublimation skips the liquid phase — solid goes straight to gas. Dry ice (solid CO₂) sublimes at room temperature; iodine crystals also sublime!

exercises.question: DEPOSITION is the opposite of sublimation. It is when ___.
choices: a gas condenses directly to a solid, skipping the liquid stage
exercises.exp: Deposition: gas → solid (no liquid stage). Frost on windows and snowflakes form by deposition — water vapour freezes directly into ice crystals!

exercises.question: In a gas, how do particles move?
choices: they stay in one spot and vibrate
they slide past each other slowly in one direction
they move rapidly and randomly in all directions, frequently colliding
they do not move at all
exercises.exp: Gas particles have so much energy they fly around in all directions randomly — frequently colliding with each other and container walls!

exercises.question: DIFFUSION is when particles spread from an area of HIGH concentration to LOW concentration. Which demonstrates diffusion?
choices: an ice cube shrinking in sunlight
the smell of baking bread spreading through a house
a rock sinking to the bottom of a pond
exercises.exp: Bread smell molecules diffuse from the kitchen (high concentration) throughout the house (low concentration) — diffusion in action!

exercises.question: Why do gases DIFFUSE faster when HEATED?
choices: heat reduces the number of particles
heating increases particle kinetic energy — particles move faster, spreading more quickly
hot particles are smaller and slip through gaps easily
exercises.exp: More thermal energy = faster particle movement = quicker diffusion. That is why food smells spread faster in a warm room than a cold one!

exercises.question: The BOILING POINT of a substance is the temperature where ___.
choices: it changes from solid to liquid
rapid evaporation occurs throughout the liquid, not just at the surface
it changes from liquid to solid
exercises.exp: At the boiling point, evaporation happens throughout the liquid (forming bubbles) — not just at the surface. 100°C for water at sea level.

exercises.question: Ice and liquid water can both exist at EXACTLY 0°C (the melting/freezing point). This is called ___.
exercises.exp: At 0°C, ice and water can coexist — both states are in thermal equilibrium. Adding heat melts more ice; removing heat freezes more water.
